title: The Monthly Dispatch — What's New in Learning Science, May 2026
author: Carl Hendrick Source: carlhendrick.substack.com
summary: Carl Hendrick's monthly research digest synthesizes 17 studies across five thematic sections of learning science, with editorial commentary that contextualizes each finding within the broader cognitive load and desirable-difficulties literature. This is a Pass A roundup PDF archiving the digest itself; the 17 linked items are primary academic research papers, not newsletter articles. Key sections: Memory, Learning, and Knowledge (7 studies); Instruction and Practice; Reading and Language Development; Motivation, Self-Regulation, and Wellbeing; Classrooms, Behaviour, and Attention; SEN and Individual Differences; and AI, Technology, and Cognitive Tools (5 studies). Standout findings: interleaving only outperforms blocked practice when combined with collaboration; the largest phone-ban study ever (5,000 schools, 35M GPS pings) shows Yondr pouches reduce phone use ~30% but have precisely zero effect on test scores; ChatGPT users scored 11 percentage points lower than traditional-method students on a 45-day retention test (the 'borrowed competence' effect); and metacognitive AI feedback produces durable transfer while affective feedback does not.
points: Interleaving's learning advantage is conditional — it only beat blocked practice when combined with collaboration on complex content; interleaving alone produced worse long-term outcomes, consistent with element-interactivity constraints from Sweller's cognitive load theory.

The largest phone-ban study ever conducted found that Yondr pouches dramatically reduced in-school phone use but had 'precisely zero' effect on standardized test scores — phone-free classrooms are a wellbeing intervention, not an academic one.

ChatGPT users in a 120-student RCT scored 57.5% vs 68.5% on a 45-day retention test: the 'borrowed competence' effect, where the AI's articulate output is mistaken for the learner's own understanding — the recommendation is to sequence AI use after initial encoding.

AI feedback that prompts metacognitive reflection produces significantly better retention and transfer; affective feedback ('great job!') shows no transfer advantage over a neutral baseline — the active ingredient is making students think harder, not feel better.

Early vocabulary strength at age 4 predicts where children start in reading comprehension but not how quickly they improve — children who started high showed less subsequent growth, suggesting comprehension gains are driven by knowledge, inferencing, and metacognition, not lexical foundation alone.
quotes: Learning that feels easy rarely lasts, and removing the productive struggle from encoding undermines consolidation. For educators, the recommendation is not to ban ChatGPT but to sequence its use. Let students attempt their own encoding first, then bring AI in as a retrieval coach or a challenge partner rather than a first-contact information source.

Phone bans appear to be a genuine wellbeing intervention — but not a learning intervention, at least not one detectable at the level of standardised test scores. This is an important distinction. Schools implementing phone policies should do so for social and developmental reasons, not because they expect results day scores to move.

Building a chatbot that says 'great job, keep going!' is not the same as building one that says 'explain back to me what you just learned and where you're still unsure.' The affective feedback felt supportive but didn't produce durable learning beyond what students would have achieved anyway.
Vocabulary is a strong predictor of where children start in reading comprehension, but a weak predictor of how quickly they improve over time.

Desirable difficulties are conditional, not universal. Interleaving benefits are strongest in lower element interactivity tasks (for example category learning or maths problem types) and weaker or negative in high complexity domains.
